question: The step definition for "Given a lesson exists in a module locked for review" can be implemented two ways: script the UI (log in, click through the lesson form, lock the module) or make two authenticated API calls (create-lesson, then lock-module). The BDD guidance firmly picks the API — for a reason beyond speed. Which?
choices: Gherkin forbids actions inside Given steps, and UI clicks are actions; API calls keep the step syntactically a precondition

A Given is scaffolding, not behaviour under test. Building preconditions through screens creates false dependencies: an unrelated redesign of a page the scenario merely passes through breaks every scenario that used it for setup. State is set up through the API, the UI is exercised only by the behaviour the scenario actually specifies — and a precondition with no API to build it is a finding to flag, not a reason to click through
UI-driven setup breaks scenario isolation, because browser state persists between scenarios while API calls are stateless
Setup through the UI makes the scenario imperative, and imperative scenarios cannot be matched by step-definition patterns
explanation: Declarative style evicts the "how" from scenarios into step definitions — and inside step definitions the same layering discipline continues: preconditions get built at the cheapest reliable layer, which is the API. The architectural argument is about coupling, not speed: a scenario that clicks through the lesson form to set up state now depends on that form's markup, so any redesign of it breaks scenarios whose subject is something else entirely — false dependencies that make the suite brittle and failures misleading. And when no API exists to build a precondition, the guidance treats that as a discovery (a missing or test-only endpoint to add) rather than a dead end. The distractors misattribute the rule: Gherkin does not police what code a step executes; isolation is the harness's job (fresh browser context and API-created data per scenario) regardless of how setup happens; and an imperative scenario matches step definitions just fine — its defect is brittleness as documentation, a different failure than this one.

question: A BDD suite has 45 Gherkin scenarios, all executed through the browser: 5 happy paths and 40 validation, permission, and limit sad paths. CI takes 50 minutes and flakes weekly. A teammate proposes deleting the sad-path scenarios and rewriting them as plain unit tests. What does the guidance actually prescribe?
choices: Keep all 45 in the browser and parallelize CI instead: acceptance scenarios are end-to-end by definition, and moving any of them off the UI layer downgrades them from acceptance tests to integration tests

Push scenarios down the pyramid without abandoning the discipline: acceptance scenarios are not chained to the top layer. Keep the happy path in the browser — one scenario per slice, proving the whole thing hangs together — and run the sad paths as the same Gherkin, at the API layer: no browser, the same specification-and-verification role, a fraction of the cost and flake
Accept the proposal: Gherkin's ceremony is only justified for the happy paths stakeholders actually read, and validation rules are implementation detail best covered by developer-facing unit tests

Collapse the 40 sad paths into a few Scenario Outlines: one scenario template with a large Examples table per rule family cuts scenario setup overhead, keeping full browser coverage at a fraction of the runtime
explanation: The pyramid rule and the BDD discipline are orthogonal, and the guidance keeps both: 'there's technically no need to write acceptance tests at the highest level — push your tests as far down the test pyramid as you can.' Gherkin's value is that the scenarios are the specification — business-readable, and drift fails the build — and that property does not depend on which layer executes the steps. Running sad paths against the API keeps every rule inside the living documentation while removing the browser's cost and flakiness; the single UI happy path still proves the slice integrates end to end. The distractors each sacrifice one half: 'acceptance means E2E' is exactly the misconception the guidance rejects; rewriting rules as unit tests silently deletes them from the living documentation, so the specification can drift from the system again without failing anything; and Scenario Outline through the UI is a named anti-pattern — each Examples row still drives the full browser flow, so the table multiplies runtime instead of cutting it.

question: A redesign replaces a form-based upload dialog with drag-and-drop. No behavior changed, yet 40 Gherkin scenarios fail — they read like 'When I click the file input / And I select "syllabus-2026.pdf" from the picker / And I click the Upload button'. The team budgets a week to update the specs. What is the actual defect, per BDD's Formulation practice?
choices: The scenarios are imperative: they encode the current UI's mechanics as if the mechanics were the specification, so a purely mechanical change reads as 40 behavioral regressions. Formulation's core style rule is declarative scenarios: the spec states what the actor accomplishes — 'When the Course Author uploads the file "syllabus-2026.pdf"' — and the clicks live in step definitions, the one layer entitled to know the UI's current shape. Rewritten declaratively, the redesign becomes an edit to one step definition, and the feature files — the living documentation — correctly show that no behavior changed. Declarative is not vague: hide the mechanics, keep the data concrete
The steps lack a page-object layer: keep the click-level steps but route every selector through page objects, so the next redesign is absorbed by updating one class instead of 40 files

Each scenario carries several When steps — a known anti-pattern signalling multiple behaviors per scenario; splitting them into single-trigger scenarios would have contained the blast radius to a handful of failures
Forty scenarios through the browser is a test-pyramid violation; re-pointing them at the API layer removes the UI dependency entirely, so no redesign can break them again
explanation: The tell is that the specification changed while the behavior didn't — for an artifact whose whole claim is 'living documentation of behavior', that is the system lying about what happened. Imperative steps are, in the docs' words, so closely tied to the mechanics of the current UI that every UI change forces a spec change; the fix is a division of labor, not better tooling: scenarios own the what (with concrete data, so they can fail meaningfully), step definitions own the how, and a redesign that preserves behavior touches only the second. The week of 'updating specs' becomes minutes of updating one step's implementation. The distractors each relocate the coupling instead of removing it: page objects deduplicate selector code, but the spec text still asserts clicks and pickers that no longer exist — the falsehood is in the language, not the locators; the multiple-When smell is real but is a symptom here — splitting imperative steps yields more, smaller imperative scenarios, every one still UI-coupled; and the pyramid guidance (happy path through the UI, sad paths at the API) optimizes cost, not correctness of expression — imperative scenarios re-pointed at an API would just couple to endpoint mechanics instead, and abandoning UI coverage because the specs were badly written treats the symptom while keeping the disease.

question: A team's canonical Gherkin lives in their design docs; a generator derives the runnable .feature files under e2e/features/. A developer spots a wrong expected total in one scenario, edits the .feature file directly, and the suite goes green. Three weeks later the generator runs and the fix silently disappears. A teammate proposes making the generator smarter — merging hand edits instead of overwriting. Per BDD's living-documentation principle, what is the actual defect?
choices: The generator's overwrite semantics: a derivation tool should merge, not clobber — a three-way merge against the last generated version preserves downstream fixes while still propagating upstream changes, the same way code formatters respect manual regions

Generating at all was the mistake: Cucumber's model makes the .feature file the specification, so the team should delete the generator, commit e2e/features/ as canonical, and let the docs link to it instead of duplicating it

The hand edit broke the derivation contract, and the green suite was the system lying. Living documentation requires exactly one canonical place where a behaviour is specified; derived copies are legitimate only while they are mechanically derived and drift-checked — never hand-edited. The fix belonged in the canonical spec, followed by regeneration: for three weeks the docs a new teammate would read still asserted the wrong total while the tests asserted the right one, and the regeneration didn't destroy the fix, it exposed that the fix had been applied to the wrong artifact. The guard is a drift check in CI — regenerate and diff — so a hand-edited derivative fails the build immediately instead of surviving until the next regeneration reverts it
A review-gate defect: regenerations should go through pull requests like any other change, where the diff reverting a bug fix would have been visible to a reviewer before it landed
explanation: The scenario tests whether you locate the failure in the tooling or in the source-of-truth discipline. Living documentation's claim is that spec and tests are the same artifact — which only holds if a behaviour has exactly one canonical home and every other copy is mechanically derived from it. The developer's edit created a fork: the derivative said one thing, the canon said another, and 'the suite is green' stopped meaning 'the spec is satisfied'. Regeneration then did its job — re-asserting the canon — and the surprise reveals the real defect: a fix applied at the wrong layer. The distractors all try to engineer around the fork instead of forbidding it. A merging generator institutionalizes two editable sources, and merging behavioural assertions is not like merging formatting — a conflict between 'total is €90' and 'total is €95' has no mechanical resolution, so drift becomes permanent and invisible. Making e2e/features/ canonical is a coherent architecture (many teams do treat feature files as canon), but it doesn't describe this team's defect: the fix landed in the derived layer while their canonical spec kept asserting the wrong number — flipping the canon after the fact just leaves the docs as the lying copy. And a PR gate on regeneration relies on a human noticing one reverted line inside a legitimate, possibly large regeneration diff — the drift check inverts that: it makes the violation fail deterministically at the moment the hand edit is made, which is where the process rule belongs.

question: A team reports it has "adopted BDD": at the end of each sprint, QA reads the shipped code and writes .feature files for it. The output is genuinely good — declarative steps, one When per scenario, files organized by domain concept, no incidental detail, green in CI, and new hires say the features are the clearest description of the system. Product and developers never attend. Judged against what BDD is for, what has this team actually built?
choices: A sound BDD practice with a sequencing flaw: the artifacts satisfy every Formulation and Automation rule, so the only cost is that the tests arrive a sprint late rather than guiding the code

A regression suite with excellent documentation, and none of BDD's actual payoff. BDD is "collaborative requirements analysis combined with test-driven development" — its value is generated during Discovery, when product, dev, and QA argue over concrete examples and surface disagreements and missing rules while changing them is still cheap. Examples derived from finished code can only ratify decisions already made and paid for: a rule nobody thought about is absent from the code, so it is absent from the features too, and the suite is green. Writing features after the code is BDD run backwards — the tests are real, but they were the by-product, never the point

A living-documentation violation: because the features are derived from the implementation rather than mechanically generated from it, they will drift from the code and the drift will not fail the build

A test-pyramid problem: post-hoc scenarios inevitably describe whatever layer the code exposes, so the suite ends up top-heavy — the fix is to re-point most of the scenarios at the API layer and keep authoring them after implementation
explanation: This tests whether you locate BDD's value in its artifacts or in the conversation that produces them. Every quality rule a reviewer can check by reading a .feature file is satisfied here, which is exactly why the question is hard: the observable output is indistinguishable from a healthy suite, and the missing half is invisible in the files. Discovery is where the return on BDD is earned — disagreement between product and developers about what "locked for review" means, or a limit nobody specified, surfaces at conversation cost instead of rework cost. Run backwards, the process is structurally incapable of that: the code is the input, so the features inherit its blind spots and then certify them as correct. The team gets regression safety and readable docs — worth having, but obtainable more cheaply and not what BDD is for. The distractors each reduce the defect to a mechanical one. Calling it a sequencing flaw treats "before implementation" as a scheduling preference rather than the mechanism that makes examples able to change the design. Drift is not the issue: these features do match the code — that is the problem, they match it unconditionally, and they will keep passing while the specification silently agrees with whatever was built. And the pyramid governs where scenarios execute, a cost-and-speed axis orthogonal to who wrote them and when; re-pointing post-hoc scenarios at the API makes a backwards process faster without making it BDD.
